steps.action:
On the northernmost tip of the island, where the rock broke the sea into white fraying teeth, the lighthouse rose out of the mist like a bone from the spine of the world.

Jonas had been its keeper for thirty-one years.

Every evening, at precisely one hour before sundown, he climbed the iron spiral that encircled the core of the tower. The steps, worn into a shallow groove by his own boots and those of the men who had come before him, ticked beneath his feet in a rhythm his body knew better than his heartbeat. Outside, the wind combed the grass flat on the cliff and drove the sound of the waves up through the stone.

At the top, he unlocked the lantern room with a key that was always slightly cold, no matter how tight he held it on the way up. The great lens—glass cut and polished a century ago in a city he had never seen—waited like a gigantic unblinking eye. Jonas moved around it, checking wicks and fuel, gears and chains. His fingers were thick and callused, but precise. He could tell, by the feel of a turned bolt, how long before it would rust through.

He lit the lamp in three motions: strike, shelter, touch. Flame flared, then steadied, the light capturing for an instant the etched ghosts of fingerprints on the glass. Outside, the dusk deepened from gray to blue to a kind of expectant purple. The first gulls wheeled homeward, their cries pulling thin threads through the air.

The light caught, thickened, and began to turn.

Jonas watched the beam sweep the sea. It cleaved the horizon, dissolved and reappeared, a revolving sentence written in brightness. Somewhere out there were the shipping lanes, the slow procession of tankers and trawlers, freighters and ferries, all depending on the sudden clean certainty of this beam when fog and current conspired to move them off their invisible rails.

He did not think of this often as dependence. It was simply his work. If the lamp went out, ships might hit the reef. If ships hit the reef, men might die. So the lamp did not go out. It was a simple equation; he was a simple man.

There had been another keeper once, in the first years: a man named Havel, his senior by decades. Havel had known every story about the sea, and some about the sky. He had whittled in the evenings, small detailed ships from driftwood, and lined them along the kitchen shelf. “So they can all come home,” he used to say without looking up, as if that explained everything and nothing.

Then one winter the fever took him. For three nights Jonas had walked halfway up the iron stair, then run back down to change wet cloths, spoon broth between chapped lips, listen to the gravel rattle in Havel’s lungs. On the fourth night a storm rose that had no business in March. The barometer dropped like a stone. Rain came in from two directions at once, and the wind screamed and twisted around the tower.

That was the night Jonas learned what it is to choose between one man and many.

He had stood in the kitchen doorway, wet hair dripping into his eyes, looking at the shape of Havel on the narrow bed and then at the black, sound-trembling well of the stair. The light had to be tended. If the lamp went dim in a storm like this, ships would not simply scrape rock—they would be torn apart, ground like shells.

Havel’s hand groped weakly across the blanket and caught Jonas’s sleeve. “Go,” the old man whispered, eyes cloudy but fierce. “You know the way. I taught you.”

Jonas went. The beam burned all night. In the gray chill that followed, when the wind dropped into a confused mutter and the rain hissed away into mist, Jonas came back down to a room that was very quiet.

He waked the body himself and rowed it to the mainland, shoulders burning with every pull of the oars. The priest said the usual words. The island said nothing. The sea, having taken its share, lay flat and innocent. When he came back alone that evening, the lighthouse was taller than it had ever been before.

From that week on, the light belonged to Jonas.

Years passed, measured in rotations of the beam and scratches added to the inside of the kitchen doorframe, each one a mark on the date of the annual inspection. The inspector came with his clipboard and his careful disinterest, was rowed from the harbor by one of the younger men. He would ask the same questions. Any trouble with the wick? Any mechanical failures? Any difficulty maintaining the glass?

“No,” Jonas would answer, and it would be almost entirely true.

The only trouble came with the fog.

Fog on the headland was not unusual. But some nights it rose in a particular way, not as a low cloud creeping over the sea but as a wall, white and dense and complete. It would swallow the cliffs, the shore, the short path from the tower to the keeper’s cottage so that one could stand in the lantern room and feel the island gone, suspended on a pedestal of nothing.

On those nights, the beam thickened into a visible blade, cutting through the milk. The foghorn, a huge iron throat below the gallery, would bellow every thirty seconds, shaking the glass, quivering Jonas’s ribs. The sound went into the fog and did not come back. The world reduced to the circle of flame, the crunch of his boots, the remembered geometry of rooms he could no longer see from outside.

Alone in the mist, Jonas sometimes thought he heard other sounds. Voices, perhaps, or the distant bell of a ship that was not there. Once, near midnight, he stepped onto the gallery and leaned into the white.

“Is anyone out there?” he called.

The foghorn answered for him, a long mournful note, and when it ended there was a second of silence so deep and close it felt like something pressing on his eardrums with padded hands. Then the sea resumed its unseen grinding below.

When letters came from the mainland—twice a month, with the supply boat—Jonas read them at the little table by the window that faced the tower. His sister wrote about the town: new shopfronts, births, marriages, the slow predictable crumbling of the church steps. The harbor master sent official notices: schedules, weather warnings, once an apology for a missed delivery when a storm had shut down the port.

He answered on thin paper, his hand cramped from the unfamiliar motion of the pen. There was not much to say. The lamp is sound. The glass is clean. I am well. The sea is the sea. Occasionally he added a particular: a whale seen breaching at dawn, slate-colored and enormous; a storm that split a pine in the old grove; a cormorant that had taken to perching on the gallery rail each morning at nine, like a punctual and disapproving neighbor.

He sent the letters back with the empty fuel drums and crates. The boatman, Tomas, took them wordlessly, his cheeks chapped and eyes watering from the spray. Once, as he pushed off, he called, “You could come in for a month, you know. They’d find a man to watch the light.”

Jonas stood on the stone step above the swell. “They’d find a man,” he agreed, and left it at that.

In the fourth decade of his service, the island changed without asking his permission.

It began with a rumor in the inspector’s mouth, let slip over a cup of coffee at Jonas’s table. “They’re talking about automating some of the old lights,” he said, flicking a crumb from his lap. “Solar panels, computer controls. It’s expensive to keep a man out here, you know.”

Jonas heard the words, but they collided with no useful shape in his mind. A lighthouse without a keeper was as absurd as a ship without a hull. Still, that night, when he climbed to light the lantern, he looked at the lamp and wondered—not for the first time, but more sharply—whether it cared who tended it.

Months went by. Letters came less often; the mainland, in a way he could not articulate, seemed to be turning its face slightly away from the sea. He noticed more lights along the distant shore at night, an orange haze that had not been there when he was young.

Then, on an oddly warm spring morning, a second boat came, larger than the supply skiff. Three men stepped out, not the usual rough shapes of fishermen but tidy figures with rolled plans and neat hair. One carried a metal case that made a dense clink when he set it down.

They shook Jonas’s hand one by one, their palms dry and brief. The oldest introduced himself as Engineer Falk. There was no inspector with them. No apology.

“Regulations have changed,” Falk said once they sat at the table, a plate of dry biscuits between them that no one touched. “We’re converting this light to automatic. You’ll be relieved of your post at the end of the week.”

Relieved. As if some weight would be lifted from him. Jonas looked at his hands, folded over one another, and said nothing.

“We’ll install sensors, a backup generator. The system is quite reliable.” Falk spoke with the confidence of a man who had practiced this conversation at other tables, on other lonely outcrops of rock. “A tender will come by once a month for maintenance.”

Jonas’s first clear thought was oddly practical. “What happens if it fails between visits?”

Falk smiled—compassion, or something like it, softening the corners of his mouth. “We have monitors now. If there’s an outage, they’ll know in the harbor office. There are redundancies. Truly, this is safer in the long run.”

Safer. The word slipped and slid across Jonas’s mind like a fish in wet hands. He had no language to argue with terminals and monitors, with the vague unassailable idea of progress. He only had the lamp, the lens, the memory of storms.

“The sea doesn’t care about your monitors,” he said finally, surprising himself with the harshness in his own voice.

For a moment, Falk’s gaze met his, steady and unreadable. Then the engineer looked away, out the small window toward the tower, as if taking the measure of a thing that, one way or another, would end up under his authority.

“It doesn’t,” Falk agreed. “That’s why the system has three backups.”

They worked for five days. Jonas watched from the path, from the kitchen, from the gallery when he felt he could not bear being below. Cables appeared where there had been none; a metal box was bolted to the stone, its face a blank unblinking panel. They attached sensors to the rotating apparatus and replaced some of the brass with steel and plastic.

At night, when the men went back to their boat to sleep, Jonas tended the light as always. The lamp did not burn differently for knowing it would soon answer to a switch a mile away rather than the strike of his match.

On the sixth day, Falk found Jonas in the lantern room, as if he had expected to. The engineer stood with his hands in his coat pockets, gaze flicking once to the slowly turning lens and back.

“It’s done,” Falk said. “From tomorrow, the control office will bring her on and off. We’ve set it to light automatically with the fall of dusk, but there will be a human operator watching the boards, if that’s any consolation.”

Jonas thought of a man in a warm room, looking at numbers on a screen. If the light went out, perhaps a red dot would appear, or a line of text would say FAULT. Somewhere a phone would ring. Someone would make a note. They might come out in the morning, if the weather allowed.

“A consolation,” he repeated, not unkindly. “No. I suppose not.”

He ran his palm along the railing one last time, feeling the familiar patches of roughness and smoothness, the places where his hand had worn the paint thin. Then he stepped back. “Will you show me?” he asked.

Falk hesitated, then nodded.

They descended the stair together. At the base of the tower, Falk opened the metal box with a key that looked, to Jonas, implausibly small. Inside were switches, rows of tiny glowing lights, a panel with a numeric display slowly incrementing the revolutions of the lens.

“This is the local override,” Falk said, touching a green button. “This one isolates the power. This is the network status. These show the generator charge.”

He spoke as if describing the weather to a stranger on a train. Jonas listened with a grave politeness. When Falk finished, they stood in a silence broken only by the distant slap of waves.

“What will you do now?” Falk asked, surprising Jonas by the question.

Jonas shrugged once, felt the motion as if it belonged to someone taller, younger. “My sister has a room. In town. I suppose I will learn which bus takes me to the market. Teach myself to sleep through the night.”

The engineer’s expression tightened, then relaxed. “The harbor has offered you a position, if you want it,” he said. “Harbor watch. You’d be… inside, mostly, monitoring the traffic systems. Screens.”

Jonas gave a short breath that might have been a laugh. “To watch the sea from behind glass, with the smell filtered out and the sound flattened?” He shook his head. “I’ve been doing much the same work for three decades. I’d only be further away from it.”

Falk looked as though he might say more, then didn’t. He closed the panel, turned the key, and held it out.

“You keep this,” he said. “Regulations say we leave a local key on-site. In case of emergencies.”

Jonas took the key. It lay on his palm, light and cool. No different in weight from the one to the lantern room, though it might as well have been from a different world.

The next evening, Jonas did not climb the stair at the accustomed hour. He stood on the path between cottage and tower, the grass whispering in the wind around his boots, and watched the sky darken. The sea was calm, its color leached to that particular heavy leaden blue that did not belong to day or night.

He waited, listening for the sound of his own footsteps on the iron that did not come.

For a moment nothing happened. Then, with a small, almost embarrassed hum from the tower, the mechanism engaged. Somewhere up there, unseen, the lamp flared to life. The beam stepped into the gathering dusk as if it had always been meant to arrive that way: suddenly, cleanly, independent of human hand.

Jonas watched it turn.

It did not falter. The light marched its steady circle, indifferent, dependable. Ships out beyond the horizon would see no difference.

He felt a hollowness open in his chest that was not quite grief and not quite relief. For all these years, his life had been a hinge between danger and safety, darkness and a thin spear of brightness. Now the hinge remained but the door no longer needed his hand to move.

In the morning, he packed.

There was less than one might think. A few clothes. A stack of letters, tied with twine. Havel’s tiny carved ships, which he wrapped one by one in strips of an old shirt. A photograph of the lighthouse taken from the sea, a gift from some long-ago visiting surveyor. The keys—lantern room and panel—he left on the kitchen table, though there was no one to turn them in to.

Before leaving, he walked the island once, from the wind-torn pines in the interior to the jag of black rock at the southern tip. He knew every dip in the path, every clump of thrift and gorse, every place where the cliff edge looked sound but crumbled easily. The island smelled of salt and kelp and the faint metallic tang of the lamp’s fuel lingering on the air.

At the very end, he went back up to the lantern room, though there was no need. The lamp was off; daylight poured through the glass like water. The lens loomed around him, multiplied reflections of his lined face and gray hair caught in the facets.

He laid his palm against the cool metal of the lamp’s housing.

“I’m leaving you in interesting company,” he said quietly, as if the machine that now watched over it could be counted as a companion. “Be kind, if you can help it.”

The mechanism, unpowered, made no answer. Far below, the sea exhaled against the rock.

On the mainland, in his sister’s narrow upstairs room, the nights were noisy. Cars passed, brakes hissing on the damp cobbles. A dog barked. Somewhere a radio played music that seemed all chorus and no verse. Jonas lay on his back and stared at the lit rectangle of the window, feeling as if he had stepped off the edge of the known chart into paper labeled only with vague dragons.

He tried the harbor job for three weeks. They sat him in front of a bank of screens, each one a flat representation of something he had once known by smell and wind and taste. Little digital icons moved across a blue field representing the sea, tagged with numbers and codes. Here, a tanker. There, a fishing boat. Lines of text at the bottom showed wind speed, visibility, barometric pressure. If something went wrong, the icons would blink, turn red, be accompanied by a polite chime.

On his third night shift he watched a storm roll in as pale green patches on the radar overlay. The waves that would be throwing themselves against the headland passed under his eyes as numerical height and period. In a small box in the corner of one screen, a label flicked briefly from LIGHTHOUSE-27: OK to LIGHTHOUSE-27: SIGNAL LOSS, then back again.

He stood up before he knew he was moving.

“Where are you going?” the younger man beside him asked, startled.

Jonas caught the back of the chair with one hand until the urge to run—out of the office, down to the harbor, into a boat that no longer waited for him—drained away enough that he could answer, “Nowhere. Just stretching my legs.”

When his shift ended at dawn, he removed the badge with his name on it and left it on the supervisor’s desk. No one tried very hard to persuade him to stay.

Seasons turned. He found small work in the town: mending nets for men too busy or too careless to do it themselves; fixing hinges on doors that the salt air had swollen; once, showing a visiting writer how to read the sky for changes in the wind. In the mornings he walked along the sea wall, watching the gulls poach scraps from the fishing boats as they came in.

Once a month, if the weather allowed, he took the ferry that passed near—but not to—the island. Regulations, again. The lighthouse was a restricted site now. Automatic or not, it belonged more firmly than ever to the system of the mainland.
